_spec.purpose: A standalone web edition of the archived visual story.
_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: UT San Antonio built a solar flood sensor that judges flood risk on the device itself. The release reports a validation score and a parts cost, and names no site and no real flood.

introduction.text: [UT San Antonio's release describes a field-ready prototype that pairs solar power with several sensors, long-range radios and machine learning on the device](c3). [The model on the node judges imminent local flood risk from current and recent readings with no central server involved](c5). [Chen Pan, an assistant professor of electrical engineering, leads the work](c13).

[The release frames the problem as timing. It says flood risk often climbs block by block, from coastal bends to low-water crossings in San Antonio, before regional alerts sound](c16). [It says some people could already have ankle-deep water in their yard when a flash flood warning reaches their phone](c17).

paragraphs.text: [The prototype carries four optical water-level sensors set at different heights](c1). [It also senses temperature, humidity, light and precipitation](c2). [A solar power system charges a built-in battery and backup energy storage](c8).

[The model runs as TinyML, which the release defines as machine learning shrunk to run on small low-power microcontrollers](c4). [Chen Pan calls the system off-grid, a design that makes its own power and judges flood risk on the device](c6).

[The node's LoRa radio reaches more than a half-mile through city streets and up to five miles in open areas, the release says](c9). [Data from many nodes is meant to reach a central site, where a second and larger model builds a dashboard with predictive maps](c10).

sections.heading: Why a reading at the crossing

paragraphs.text: [The release says regional weather models and satellite imaging can miss very local flash floods](c18). A separate study points the same way. [UT Arlington researchers compared radar with more than {{number:c20}} rain gauges and found standard radar can underestimate storm totals by roughly {{number:c20:1}} under some conditions](c20). [UT Arlington's Water Engineering Research Center is building a rainfall monitoring and flood modeling system for Hill Country early warning](c21).

[The release reports {{number:c7}} validation accuracy in initial assessments after training](c7). That is a score measured on data. It is not a count of floods the node caught. [Parts for one prototype station cost roughly ${{number:c11}} to ${{number:c11:1}}](c11). [Chen Pan is seeking a patent on the hardware, and the team aims to turn the prototype into a weatherized commercial product](c12). [The release says the design is meant for small coastal towns](c19).

[The release names no installation site, no city or county operating the system, no field test against a real flood and no false alarm or missed event figure](c19). A reader can't tell from it how the node behaves when water actually rises at a crossing, or how often it would warn when no flood comes.

The stakes at the water are already measured elsewhere. [The National Weather Service cites the CDC as reporting that more than half of flood-related drownings happen when a vehicle is driven into flood water](c22). Whatever a sensor on the post reports, the decision at the edge of the water stays with the driver.
